title: Five of the six families promised an investigation following the deaths of their babies have been excluded from the official review.
text_ai: In November, the health secretary ordered a review of the "unnecessary" deaths of six babies at Crosshouse hospital in Ayrshire since 2008. But the BBC has learned it will only look at cases that have happened since December 2013. The review is being carried out by Healthcare Improvement Scotland (HIS). This significant narrowing of scope means that only one of the six families initially promised a thorough examination of their child's death will now have their case scrutinised by HIS. The decision has left the five excluded families reeling, expressing profound disappointment and a sense of betrayal, stating that the very purpose of the review – to provide answers and accountability for their "unnecessary" losses – has been fundamentally undermined. Mrs. Sarah Jenkins, whose son Thomas died at Crosshouse in 2010 due to complications during labour, described her reaction as "utter devastation and disbelief." Speaking exclusively to the BBC, Mrs. Jenkins said, "When the Health Secretary announced the review, we finally felt a glimmer of hope. We were promised a comprehensive investigation into why our baby died, why our lives were shattered. Now, to be told they won't even look at Thomas's case because it happened 'too long ago' feels like they’re trying to sweep us under the carpet. It’s a cruel mockery of our grief." The initial announcement in November by the then Health Secretary, made following sustained pressure from affected families and local politicians, explicitly referred to "six babies" who had died at the hospital "since 2008." The language used at the time gave the strong impression that all these cases would be included. However, correspondence seen by the BBC reveals that HIS has now informed the families that its remit is strictly limited to incidents occurring from December 2013 onwards. This cutoff date effectively excludes all but one of the cases that prompted the original inquiry. Healthcare Improvement Scotland, the independent body tasked with ensuring the quality and safety of healthcare in Scotland, confirmed the scope of the review to the BBC. A spokesperson stated, "The remit for the review into maternity and neonatal services at NHS Ayrshire & Arran was set by the Health Secretary following a request from the health board. This review, which is currently underway, focuses on events from December 2013 onwards, as this is when a new model of care was introduced at Crosshouse hospital. The purpose is to assess current practices and identify lessons to ensure future improvements in patient safety and care." This explanation, however, has done little to assuage the anger of the excluded families. Mr. David Henderson, whose daughter, Emily, died in 2011 after a critical delay in her transfer to another unit, questioned the reasoning. "How can you learn lessons for future care if you ignore the historical failings that led to the deaths of our children?" he asked. "The problems we experienced didn't just vanish in 2013. They are part of a continuum. To say that a 'new model of care' somehow erases the need to understand what went wrong before is a bureaucratic excuse, not a genuine commitment to justice or improvement." The original intervention by the Health Secretary came after years of campaigning by the families, who felt their concerns had not been adequately addressed by NHS Ayrshire & Arran. Their collective stories painted a troubling picture of missed opportunities, communication breakdowns, and a lack of transparency following the deaths of their infants. The promise of a ministerial review was seen as a significant victory, signalling a higher level of scrutiny and a potential pathway to answers they had long been denied. The five cases now excluded from the HIS review are: * **Thomas Jenkins (2010):** Died shortly after birth due to complications during a prolonged labour, with questions raised about foetal monitoring. * **Emily Henderson (2011):** Died following an emergency transfer that was allegedly delayed, leading to a critical deterioration in her condition. * **Chloe McGregor (2009):** Died from a suspected infection that parents believe was not diagnosed or treated promptly enough. * **Baby Boy Campbell (2012):** Died unexpectedly in the neonatal unit, with parents seeking clarity on the care provided in the hours leading up to his death. * **Sophia Davies (2008):** Died as a result of a rare but treatable condition that was allegedly missed during antenatal and early postnatal care. The single case that *will* be reviewed by HIS is that of baby Liam Fraser, who died in 2014, with parents having raised concerns about staffing levels and the management of a specific medical condition. While Liam's parents welcome the review of their son's case, they too expressed solidarity with the other families. "No family should go through what we have, and every family deserves answers," said Mrs. Fiona Fraser. "It feels wrong that some are included and others are not, especially when the initial promise was so clear." The BBC has also learned that the Health Secretary's original letter to NHS Ayrshire & Arran in November, which formally requested the review, made specific mention of "a number of cases of infant deaths since 2008." While it did not explicitly state *all* cases would be reviewed, the families contend that the spirit and public messaging of the announcement strongly implied a broader scope. A spokesperson for the Scottish Government declined to comment on the specific discussions that led to the definition of the HIS remit, stating only that "the Health Secretary acted on advice from officials and HIS regarding the most effective way to address concerns and ensure future patient safety." This explanation has been met with incredulity by patient advocacy groups. Dr. Eleanor Vance, director of 'Parents for Patient Safety Scotland', called the decision "unacceptable." "To offer hope to grieving families, and then to snatch it away with a technicality, is not only cruel but undermines public trust in the review process," Dr. Vance told the BBC. "The purpose of such an investigation should be to understand systemic failings, not just those that fall neatly within an arbitrary timeframe. Lessons from 2008 or 2010 are just as vital as lessons from 2014, especially in areas like staff training, communication protocols, and diagnostic pathways, which often evolve slowly." The controversy also raises questions about the role of NHS Ayrshire & Arran. Prior to the ministerial intervention, the health board had conducted its own internal reviews into some of these deaths. However, families consistently expressed dissatisfaction with the thoroughness and independence of these internal processes, leading them to escalate their concerns to the Scottish Government. Critics argue that limiting the HIS review allows the health board to avoid a comprehensive re-examination of its historical practices and accountability for earlier failings. When approached for comment, NHS Ayrshire & Arran reiterated its commitment to patient safety. A spokesperson said, "NHS Ayrshire & Arran continues to offer its deepest condolences to all families who have experienced the tragic loss of a baby. We fully cooperate with Healthcare Improvement Scotland in its ongoing review of maternity and neonatal services. We acknowledge the distress that any limitation on a review's scope can cause, and we remain committed to engaging with all families to address their ongoing concerns through appropriate channels." However, the health board did not specify what "appropriate channels" would be available to the five excluded families, nor did it commit to initiating further independent reviews of their cases. Political figures have been quick to condemn the development. Jackie Baillie MSP, Scottish Labour's Shadow Health Secretary, described the situation as "a shocking betrayal of grieving parents." She told the BBC, "The Health Secretary promised a full, comprehensive review into the 'unnecessary' deaths of six babies. To then narrow the scope to exclude five of those families is an insult to their pain and a complete dereliction of duty. It suggests a deliberate attempt to avoid confronting the full extent of past failings. The Health Secretary must immediately intervene to broaden the scope of this review to include all six families, as was originally promised." The Scottish Liberal Democrats’ health spokesperson, Alex Cole-Hamilton MSP, echoed these sentiments, stating, "This is not how we treat families who have suffered unimaginable loss. Transparency and accountability are paramount. If the government is truly committed to learning lessons and improving care, it cannot simply draw a line in the sand and ignore the cases that fall outside a convenient timeframe. This decision will only deepen the mistrust families have in the system." The emotional toll on the excluded families is immense. Mrs. Jenkins described how the initial announcement of the review had given her a sense of purpose after years of despair. "I felt like Thomas's short life would finally mean something, that his death would lead to change and prevent other families from suffering," she explained, her voice heavy with emotion. "Now, that hope has been extinguished. It feels like we're back to square one, fighting alone against a system that doesn't want to look at its own past." For families like the Campbells, whose baby boy died in 2012, the situation is particularly galling. "We were told repeatedly by the health board that everything possible was done," said Mr. Campbell. "But we never truly believed it. We thought this independent review would finally give us the objective answers we needed. To be told now that our son's death is not relevant to 'current practices' is an affront to his memory and to our enduring pain." The process of HIS reviews typically involves a deep dive into clinical records, interviews with staff, and an assessment against national standards and best practice guidelines. While the focus is often on systemic improvements rather than individual blame, the findings can be crucial for families seeking to understand what happened and to ensure similar tragedies are prevented. By limiting the scope, critics argue that HIS is being prevented from identifying patterns of failure that might have existed across a longer period and could still inform current practices. The families are now considering their next steps, including potential legal challenges to the decision and renewed calls for the Health Secretary to intervene personally. "We won't give up," Mrs. Henderson asserted. "Emily deserves answers, and so do Thomas, Chloe, Baby Campbell, and Sophia. We were promised a review of *our* babies' deaths, and we will continue to fight until that promise is honoured." This latest development casts a shadow over the Scottish Government's commitment to patient safety and transparency, particularly in sensitive areas like maternity and neonatal care. As the HIS review proceeds with its limited remit, the five excluded families remain in limbo, their hopes for justice and understanding once again dashed, leaving fundamental questions unanswered about accountability for the "unnecessary" deaths of their children at Crosshouse hospital. The pressure on the Health Secretary to revisit this decision and ensure a truly comprehensive investigation is now intensifying.

title: A parachutist who died after spiralling out of control was knocked unconscious when the parachute opened too quickly, an inquest heard.
text_ai: Chris Jones, 61, died of multiple injuries after hitting the ground on a jump from 6,000ft (1,800m). He packed the parachute himself and died at Dunkeswell Aerodrome near Honiton, Devon, in July. The Coroner Dr Elizabeth Erland passed a narrative verdict. The inquest in Exeter heard that Mr Jones, a highly experienced skydiver with over 1,000 jumps, was rendered unconscious moments after deploying his main parachute. Evidence presented by the British Skydiving Association (BSA) indicated that the canopy's rapid deployment, possibly due to a packing error or an unusual air current, caused a severe jolt. This sudden deceleration and impact force led to a "significant head injury" that incapacitated him instantly. Witnesses on the ground, including fellow skydivers and aerodrome staff, described seeing Mr Jones's parachute open before he began an uncontrolled spiral towards the ground. Despite the main canopy being fully deployed, he made no attempt to steer it or deploy his reserve parachute. Instructor Paul Smith told the court: "It was clear something was wrong. He was just hanging there, limp, not reacting. It was absolutely horrific to watch." The post-mortem examination confirmed that Mr Jones sustained extensive trauma consistent with a high-impact fall. Dr Erland concluded that the immediate unconsciousness prevented Mr Jones from taking any corrective action, such as attempting to deploy his reserve parachute. Experts clarified that his automatic activation device (AAD), designed to deploy a reserve at a critical altitude, would not have activated because the main canopy was already open, despite being uncontrolled. Mr Jones, a retired engineer from Exeter, had been a regular at Dunkeswell Aerodrome for many years and was known for his meticulous approach to the sport. He had meticulously packed his own parachute, a common practice among experienced skydivers. The inquest heard that while the packing technique itself was not definitively faulted, the combination of factors led to an unusually aggressive opening. In her narrative verdict, Dr Erland emphasised the tragic and unforeseen nature of the incident. She stated that while skydiving inherently carries risks, this particular sequence of events was a rare occurrence. The coroner did not identify any systemic failures but highlighted the importance of continued vigilance in safety protocols within the sport. title: A recent drought shut down the Amazon Basin's carbon sink by killing trees and slowing trees' growth rates, a study has shown.

Such a scenario would have catastrophic implications for global climate stability, making it considerably harder to meet international climate targets set under agreements like the Paris Accord. title: European leaders are billing their new proposal to deal with the refugee and migrant influx as a "game-changer", but the scheme is not agreed yet and there are doubts about whether it it is practical or even legal.
text_ai: The centrepiece is a plan to take any refugees and migrants who cross the sea to Greece in smugglers' boats and return them, directly, to Turkey. Critics, including the United Nations refugee agency (UNHCR) and numerous human rights organisations, argue that Turkey does not currently meet these criteria. Turkey has ratified the 1951 Refugee Convention but maintains a geographical limitation, meaning it only grants full refugee status to those fleeing conflict in Europe. This process alone could overwhelm the already strained Greek asylum system. The proposed deal would require Greece to rapidly process asylum claims on its islands, conducting eligibility interviews and identifying those to be returned. This would necessitate a significant deployment of asylum experts, judges, and interpreters – resources Greece currently lacks. The European Asylum Support Office (EASO) would be expected to provide hundreds of personnel, but even with this assistance, the speed required to make the scheme a deterrent seems almost insurmountable. For Turkey, the deal offers substantial incentives. In exchange for taking back all irregular migrants from Greece, the EU has offered an additional €3 billion in aid, on top of the €3 billion already pledged, to help care for the 2.7 million Syrian refugees currently living within its borders. Furthermore, Turkey is pushing for accelerated visa liberalisation for its citizens traveling to the Schengen area, with a target date of June 2016, and a re-energising of its stalled EU accession talks. These political concessions are highly controversial among some EU member states, particularly regarding visa-free travel, given concerns about Turkey's human rights record, including press freedom and its treatment of Kurdish minorities. The prospect of Turkey gaining greater leverage in its relationship with the EU has also raised eyebrows. Critics argue that the EU is effectively outsourcing its refugee crisis to a country with a questionable human rights record, potentially compromising its values for the sake of political expediency. Human rights groups have documented instances of Syrian refugees being pushed back at the Turkish border or held in detention centres without due process. Ensuring that those returned from Greece are treated humanely and have access to effective protection mechanisms will be a significant challenge. The "one-for-one" resettlement aspect of the plan also faces practical difficulties. While intended to create a legal alternative to irregular migration, it relies on the willingness of EU member states to take in a significant number of Syrian refugees directly from Turkey. Many countries are already struggling with the integration of asylum seekers who arrived last year, and political appetite for further large-scale resettlement remains limited, particularly in Eastern European nations. This raises concerns about whether the "one-for-one" mechanism can be scaled up sufficiently to match the number of returns, or if it will simply lead to more people being stuck in Turkey. Chancellor Angela Merkel has staked considerable political capital on finding a European solution. The proposed deal with Turkey is seen as a last-ditch effort to prevent the complete collapse of the Schengen agreement and the return of national border controls across the continent. Ultimately, the success of the "game-changer" proposal hinges on a delicate balance: addressing the humanitarian imperative, upholding international law, and satisfying the diverse political demands of 28 member states and a powerful neighbouring country. The doubts about its practicality and legality are not merely academic; they represent fundamental challenges that could derail the entire scheme, leaving Europe's refugee crisis as intractable as ever. It's a night that will live with us forever, and it's a testament to the character and spirit of this football club." Across the dugout, Barcelona manager Tito Vilanova cut a philosophical figure. While gracious in defeat, acknowledging Celtic's passion and defensive resolve, he also pointed to his side's inability to convert their overwhelming possession into clear-cut chances. "We had the ball, we created opportunities, but we couldn't score," Vilanova conceded, a hint of frustration in his tone. "Celtic defended very well, very compact, and their goalkeeper made some excellent saves. We made mistakes for their goals, and at this level, you get punished. It's a difficult result for us, but we must learn from it and focus on the next game. The group is still open." Indeed, the result sent shockwaves through Group G, dramatically altering the landscape of qualification for the knockout stages. Prior to kick-off, Barcelona were widely expected to cruise through, with Celtic battling Spartak Moscow and Benfica for the second spot. This astonishing victory, however, propelled Celtic into a commanding position, giving them a genuine belief that they could achieve something truly special in this Champions League campaign. It was a result that reverberated across European football, a stark reminder that even the most dominant forces can be humbled by a combination of tactical brilliance, unwavering spirit, and the electrifying atmosphere of a truly special stadium. Historically, this victory immediately takes its place among Celtic's most cherished European nights. Comparisons were quickly drawn to the famous Lisbon Lions triumph of 1967, and other memorable upsets such as the victory over Leeds United in the 1970 European Cup semi-final, or the thrilling draw against Juventus in 2001. While not a final or a semi-final, the sheer stature of the opponent – a Barcelona side widely regarded as one of the greatest club teams of all time – elevated this win to an almost mythical status. It was a victory for the underdog, a triumph of heart and endeavour over seemingly insurmountable talent and resources. The impact of this result extends beyond the immediate group standings. It instilled a renewed sense of pride and self-belief within the Celtic squad, demonstrating that they could compete with, and indeed beat, the very best on the grandest stage. For the supporters, it was a validation of their unwavering loyalty and passion, a night where their collective voice truly felt like the twelfth man. The scenes of celebration in Glasgow, with fans spilling out of pubs and onto the streets, painted a vivid picture of the sheer joy and significance of the achievement. Looking ahead, Celtic now face the challenge of maintaining this momentum. The remaining group stage fixtures, while still difficult, will be approached with a newfound confidence. The psychological barrier of facing Europe's elite has been dismantled, replaced by the knowledge that on their day, and with their supporters behind them, anything is possible. For Barcelona, it serves as a wake-up call, a reminder that even their unparalleled talent requires absolute focus and clinical execution to succeed at the highest level. In the annals of European football, there are nights that transcend the ordinary, moments where the script is torn up and rewritten by sheer force of will and a touch of magic. This was one such night. Celtic, the Glasgow giants, had not just beaten Barcelona; they had defied expectations, challenged perceptions, and delivered a performance that will be discussed, replayed, and celebrated for generations to come. It was a night when David truly conquered Goliath, when belief triumphed over budgets, and when the thunderous roar of Celtic Park once again echoed across the continent, proclaiming the enduring power of football's greatest upsets.

title: For the past 16 years, the electoral map for US presidential elections has been variations on a familiar theme.
text_ai: Ohio and Florida are the key battlegrounds. A handful of other states - including New Hampshire, Virginia, Colorado and Iowa - count as smaller prizes in the quest to the reach the magic number of 270 electoral votes. For much of that period, the pathway to the presidency for both major parties hinged on their ability to capture these pivotal states. Ohio, with its diverse industrial and agricultural landscape, and Florida, a mosaic of retirees, Latino communities, and military families, were seen as microcosms of the national electorate. Their results were often predictive of the overall outcome, making them the relentless focus of campaign advertising, candidate visits, and ground operations. The smaller prizes, like Virginia and Colorado, once reliably Republican but trending purple, offered additional routes, while New Hampshire and Iowa, with their distinct political cultures, provided opportunities for either party to chip away at their opponent’s electoral advantage. However, beneath the surface of this familiar electoral terrain, powerful demographic and economic currents have been reshaping the American political landscape, gradually redrawing the battle lines for presidential contests. What was once a relatively stable map, defined by a handful of swing states, is now undergoing a more fundamental transformation, presenting both Republicans and Democrats with new opportunities and significant challenges. Perhaps the most striking development has been the emergence of the "Sun Belt" states as critical new battlegrounds, shifting the electoral gravity southward and westward. Arizona and Georgia, historically pillars of Republican strength, have become fiercely competitive. In Arizona, rapid population growth, driven by an influx of younger, more diverse residents, particularly from California, combined with a growing Latino electorate and a suburban shift away from traditional Republicanism, has turned the state purple. The 2020 election saw it narrowly flip Democratic for the first time in decades, a trend reinforced by subsequent Senate races. Analysts suggest this transformation is not merely cyclical but indicative of a long-term demographic evolution that makes the state a perennial target for both parties. Similarly, Georgia, once considered a reliably red state, has witnessed a remarkable political metamorphosis. The burgeoning Black electorate, particularly around the Atlanta metropolitan area, coupled with the increasing diversity and liberal leanings of its fast-growing suburbs, has created a potent Democratic coalition. Grassroots organising, voter registration efforts, and a changing perception of the Democratic party among younger voters and educated professionals have been instrumental in this shift. Like Arizona, Georgia delivered its electoral votes to the Democratic candidate in 2020 and subsequently elected two Democratic senators, signalling its firm entrenchment as a key swing state. While Arizona and Georgia represent the most dramatic recent shifts, other states are also feeling the tremors of this evolving map. North Carolina, a state with a complex blend of growing urban centres, conservative rural areas, and a significant African American population, has consistently hovered on the edge of becoming a true swing state. Though it has largely remained Republican in presidential contests, the margins have often been exceedingly narrow, making it a persistent target for Democratic investment and a state where both parties must campaign vigorously. Its demographic trends, particularly the growth of its research triangle cities, suggest it could follow the path of Virginia, which transitioned from a swing state to a reliably Democratic one over the past two decades. Meanwhile, the traditional "Blue Wall" states of Pennsylvania, Michigan, and Wisconsin, which unexpectedly flipped to Donald Trump in 2016, have re-emerged as fiercely contested battlegrounds. These states, once seen as Democratic strongholds due to their strong labour union presence and working-class populations, revealed a deep vein of economic anxiety and cultural resentment that proved fertile ground for populist appeals. The 2020 election saw them return to the Democratic column, but often by razor-thin margins, underscoring their continued volatility. The urban-rural divide, the decline of manufacturing, and the ongoing debate over trade and globalisation continue to shape their political leanings, making them indispensable to any path to 270 electoral votes. Concurrently, some of the traditional battlegrounds have begun to drift out of the spotlight, either becoming more reliably partisan or simply less decisive. Ohio, once the quintessential swing state, has trended increasingly Republican in recent cycles. While still capable of producing close statewide races, its presidential electoral votes have consistently favoured Republicans since 2012, often by significant margins. Analysts attribute this shift to a combination of factors, including a changing industrial landscape, a decline in union membership, and a strong resonance of populist conservative messages with its working-class white population. The state, once a bellwether, now appears to lean more consistently to the right. Similarly, Iowa, a smaller prize in the past, has also shown a pronounced Republican tilt in recent presidential elections. Its agricultural base and increasingly conservative rural electorate have made it a difficult proposition for Democrats, despite its historical role in the presidential primary process. Florida, while still capable of delivering close results, has also demonstrated a recent shift, albeit a complex one. After decades of being the ultimate swing state, its electoral votes have gone Republican in the last two presidential elections, often by larger margins than previously seen. This trend is attributed to several factors: a significant influx of new residents, many of whom are retirees from other Republican-leaning states; the growing Republican strength among certain segments of the Latino electorate, particularly Cuban Americans and some Venezuelan and Colombian communities; and a robust Republican ground game that has proven highly effective in mobilising its base. While Democrats still view it as a potential target, the state’s increasingly red hue at the presidential level suggests it may no longer be the dead-centre battleground it once was. On the other hand, the states that were once considered smaller prizes for *both* parties have now largely solidified their partisan leanings. Virginia, Colorado, and New Hampshire, all once hotly contested, have become increasingly reliable Democratic states. Virginia's transformation is particularly stark, driven by the rapid growth and diversification of its northern suburbs, home to a highly educated, affluent, and increasingly diverse population. Colorado has followed a similar trajectory, with its urban centres and booming tech industry drawing in a younger, more liberal demographic. New Hampshire, while still capable of electing Republicans to statewide office, has consistently voted Democratic in presidential elections, reflecting its distinct political culture and growing suburban population. These states, while still requiring attention, are no longer the toss-ups they once were, forcing Democrats to look elsewhere for their marginal gains. The underlying forces driving these seismic shifts are multifaceted. Demographics play a critical role, with the growth of diverse populations – Latino, Asian American, and younger voters – reshaping electorates. Urbanisation and suburbanisation continue to be powerful engines of change; as cities expand and suburbs diversify, they often lean more Democratic, while rural areas tend to remain conservative. The educational divide has also become a defining feature of American politics, with college-educated voters increasingly aligning with the Democratic Party, and non-college-educated voters, particularly white working-class men, gravitating towards the Republican Party. Furthermore, political realignment, significantly accelerated by the Trump era, has fundamentally altered party coalitions. The Republican Party, under Donald Trump, solidified its hold on a segment of the white working class and rural voters, while the Democratic Party strengthened its appeal among educated suburbanites, urban populations, and minority groups. This realignment has meant that the issues that resonate most powerfully with voters have also shifted, moving beyond traditional economic concerns to encompass cultural grievances, identity politics, and differing visions of America's future. The implications for future presidential elections are profound. Campaign strategies must now adapt to a more geographically diverse and politically complex battleground. Candidates can no longer solely focus on the familiar two or three swing states. Instead, they must build broader coalitions across a wider array of states, some of which were once considered out of reach. This requires significant investment in ground operations, advertising, and messaging tailored to the specific nuances of each new competitive state. For Democrats, the emergence of Arizona and Georgia provides new and potentially more stable pathways to the White House, offsetting losses in states like Ohio and Iowa. However, maintaining these gains requires sustained engagement with diverse communities and persuasive messaging that resonates with both urban and suburban voters. For Republicans, the challenge is to prevent further erosion in the Sun Belt while solidifying their base in traditionally conservative areas and continuing to compete fiercely in the Midwest. The party must find ways to appeal to a broader electorate without alienating its core supporters. The magic number of 270 electoral votes remains the ultimate prize, but the map to reach it is no longer the familiar, relatively static puzzle it was for much of the early 21st century. The electoral landscape is now a dynamic, fluid entity, constantly being reshaped by demographic tides, economic shifts, and evolving political loyalties. The era of predictable swing states, where Ohio and Florida held undisputed sway, appears to be drawing to a close, giving way to a more complex and potentially more volatile electoral future, where presidential contests will be fought across a broader and less predictable array of battlegrounds. This transformation ensures that every election cycle will offer a fresh test of both parties' ability to adapt, innovate, and connect with an ever-changing American electorate.

title: Champions Ivory Coast twice pegged back DR Congo to earn a 2-2 draw and keep alive their hopes of reaching the Africa Cup of Nations quarter-finals.

title: A series of programmes aimed at stopping radical Islamists from joining the fighting in countries like Iraq and Syria is being launched in the US.

title: A retired police general is going on trial in Colombia for his alleged role in the 1989 murder of presidential candidate Luis Carlos Galan.
text_ai: Gen Miguel Maza Marquez was the head of Colombia's now defunct spy agency DAS at the time of Mr Galan's murder. title: Chancellor Angela Merkel has come under pressure from her coalition partner to disclose a list of spying targets given to German intelligence (BND) by the US.
text_ai: Vice Chancellor Sigmar Gabriel was responding to claims that the BND had helped the US National Security Agency (NSA) spy on German firms. title: David Cameron has been feeling the wrath of Twitter after saying in a speech that he supported West Ham when he is an Aston Villa fan.

title: Donald Trump has said the United States will "solve" the nuclear threat from North Korea, with or without China's help.

President Trump has criticised China for not doing enough to rein in its neighbour, suggesting Beijing could exert greater economic pressure. title: Pregnant women should ensure they have the whooping cough jab to protect their babies, Public Health England is urging.

title: George Bernard Shaw once said that "censorships exist to prevent anyone from challenging current conceptions and existing institutions".

When media outlets are intimidated into silence or self-censorship, the public's access to vital information is curtailed, and the space for critical thinking shrinks. While the rise of social media has offered alternative platforms for expression, these too have become battlegrounds. Governments increasingly seek to regulate online content, often citing the spread of misinformation or hate speech, but critics fear these powers can also be used to silence dissenting voices. The ongoing debate in India, ignited by the notices to the TV networks, thus reflects a fundamental struggle over the very definition of freedom of expression and the limits of state power in a democratic society. It asks whether the "current conceptions" of justice and national interest are open to scrutiny, or if, as Shaw suggested, censorship is merely a tool to ensure they remain unchallenged.

His strategy of focusing on economic inequality and railing against the "billionaire class" has resonated deeply with younger voters and working-class Americans, but he must demonstrate an ability to connect with a broader swath of the electorate. This shortfall often sees science lessons being squeezed out by a greater focus on core subjects like English and Maths, particularly in the run-up to Key Stage 2 SATs. According to the study, the perceived lack of priority for science manifests in various ways, including reduced time allocations, a scarcity of dedicated equipment, and insufficient professional development for staff. The finding that a third of primary teachers feel unconfident teaching science is a key concern for the CBI. Primary teachers are typically generalists, responsible for delivering a broad curriculum, and without regular, subject-specific training, many feel ill-equipped to deliver engaging and challenging science lessons that go beyond textbook learning. Education Secretary Gillian Keegan, responding to the report, dismissed its findings robustly. "To suggest that science is being squeezed out of primary schools is simply nonsense," she stated. "Our new, knowledge-rich curriculum places a strong emphasis on science from the earliest years, ensuring children develop a deep understanding of the world around them through practical experiments and theoretical knowledge. It rivals the best in the world, and we are seeing excellent progress." The Department for Education highlighted the government's investment in science education initiatives, including the Primary Science Quality Mark and continued professional development opportunities for teachers, citing an increase in the number of science specialists in schools. However, independent educational researchers and professional bodies echoed some of the CBI's concerns. Dr. Emily Watkins, head of primary education at the Institute of Education, commented: "While the curriculum itself may be ambitious, its effective delivery relies heavily on confident, well-resourced teachers. The Royal Society also weighed in, stressing the importance of early engagement with science. A spokesperson said: "Igniting a passion for science at primary level is fundamental for nurturing future innovators and ensuring a scientifically literate populace. The CBI report suggests this trend could have long-term implications for the UK's future workforce, potentially leading to a shortage of skilled individuals in science, technology, engineering, and mathematics (STEM) sectors. Furthermore, the report calls for greater collaboration between schools and local businesses to bring real-world science into the classroom. The differing perspectives highlight an ongoing debate about curriculum breadth and resource allocation in England's primary schools. While the government maintains its robust curriculum provides a strong foundation, the CBI and other experts argue that without sufficient time, confidence, and resources, the ambitious goals for primary science education risk remaining largely aspirational. The challenge, it seems, lies not just in what is taught, but how it is delivered and prioritised in a busy school week.

title: Philip Hammond has defended the UK's burgeoning commercial links with China, saying they are investing in the UK for financial not political reasons.

"Science takes things apart to see how they work. Religion puts things together to see what they mean," he has often explained, suggesting that while science explores the universe as a problem to be solved, religion understands it as a mystery to be lived. "Rabbi Sacks has built a reputation as a moral voice for our time, one who can articulate a compelling vision of faith that is both intellectually rigorous and deeply compassionate," she stated. The Templeton Prize, established in 1972 by the late global investor and philanthropist Sir John Templeton, aims to honour living persons who have made exceptional contributions to affirming life's spiritual dimension, whether through insight, discovery, or practical works. Previous recipients include Mother Teresa, Desmond Tutu, and the Dalai Lama, placing Lord Sacks among a distinguished cohort of individuals recognised for their profound impact on humanity's search for meaning and purpose. title: Fox News' most popular show is facing an exodus of advertisers because of sexual harassment claims against its host, Bill O'Reilly.

title: Scientists have begun to predict the animals that may become extinct in the next century because of climate change.
text_ai: Researchers at Brown University in the US have combined predictions of climate change with the geographic ranges of well-studied amphibians. While the animals will try to migrate to areas with more suitable weather, short-term temperature fluctuations can cut them off. The findings suggest more effort should be made to relocate vulnerable species. The study, published in the journal *Nature Climate Change*, focused on hundreds of species of frogs, toads, and salamanders across North and South America. These cold-blooded creatures are particularly sensitive to shifts in temperature and humidity, making them crucial indicators of broader ecological stress. Dr. Sarah Jenkins, lead author and an ecological modeller at Brown, explained that while previous research often focused on long-term climate trends, their new model integrated high-frequency, short-duration extreme weather events. "It's not just about a species needing to move 100 miles north over 50 years," Dr. Jenkins stated in a press briefing. "It's about whether they can survive a two-week heatwave or an unseasonal cold snap that isolates them from food sources or breeding grounds, effectively creating 'climate traps'." The research highlighted that even if a species possesses the theoretical ability to migrate to cooler climes, these sudden, intense fluctuations could render their path impassable or decimate populations before they can reach a new, stable habitat. The findings resonate with growing concerns across the scientific community about the vulnerability of a wide array of species. While amphibians often serve as a bellwether, other groups, from insects to large mammals, are also under increasing threat. A separate report by the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC) warned that up to a million species face extinction, many within decades, if global warming continues unchecked. Polar bears, iconic symbols of the Arctic, are already struggling as sea ice melts, limiting their hunting grounds. Coral reefs, vital marine ecosystems, are experiencing unprecedented bleaching events due to rising ocean temperatures and acidification. Even seemingly adaptable species, like some migratory birds, are facing disrupted breeding cycles and food availability as their traditional routes and timings become out of sync with shifting seasons. The suggestion to relocate vulnerable species, while offering a glimmer of hope, presents significant logistical and ethical hurdles. "Assisted migration, or 'managed relocation', is a highly complex conservation strategy," commented Professor Mark Davies, an expert in conservation biology at the University of Oxford, who was not involved in the Brown study. "It's not simply a matter of moving animals from A to B." Scientists must carefully assess the new habitat's suitability, considering not only climate but also food sources, predators, and potential diseases that could be introduced, harming existing ecosystems. There's also the question of genetic diversity within relocated populations and the long-term sustainability of such interventions. Critics argue that while it may be necessary in extreme cases, it risks creating 'ecological refugees' and could distract from the fundamental need to address the root causes of climate change. Alongside potential relocation efforts, conservationists are increasingly focusing on creating "climate corridors" – networks of protected habitats that allow species to move more freely as their environments shift. These corridors aim to facilitate natural migration, offering pathways through fragmented landscapes often disrupted by human development. Restoring degraded habitats, managing invasive species, and reducing other human pressures like pollution and deforestation are also crucial. These measures can bolster the resilience of ecosystems, making them better equipped to cope with the stresses of a changing climate. The concept of 'rewilding' – returning landscapes to a more natural state – is also gaining traction, with proponents arguing it can create more robust and adaptable environments for wildlife. Ultimately, scientists stress that while adaptation strategies like relocation and corridors are important, they are only partial solutions. The primary driver of these extinctions remains the rapid, human-induced alteration of the global climate. "No amount of species shuffling will negate the need for aggressive greenhouse gas emission reductions," emphasised Dr. Jenkins. International agreements, such as the Paris Agreement, aim to limit global warming to well below 2°C, preferably to 1.5°C, above pre-industrial levels. Achieving these targets requires a rapid transition away from fossil fuels, significant investment in renewable energy, and sustainable land use practices. The scale of the challenge is immense, demanding coordinated global action from governments, industries, and individuals. The implications of widespread species extinction extend far beyond the loss of individual animals. Ecosystems are interconnected webs; the disappearance of one species can have cascading effects, disrupting food chains, pollination services, and nutrient cycles that are essential for human well-being. From the medicines derived from rainforest plants to the clean water provided by healthy wetlands, biodiversity underpins many of the planet's life-support systems. The research from Brown University serves as a stark reminder that the window for meaningful intervention is rapidly closing. Scientists hope that by identifying the most vulnerable species and the precise mechanisms of their decline, more targeted and effective conservation efforts can be deployed, buying precious time for some of the planet's most unique and irreplaceable inhabitants. The future of countless species, they warn, hinges on the decisions made in the coming years.

title: Grand Theft Auto's creator Take-Two Interactive has shut down three hugely popular tools that let players alter features and cheat at the game.

title: Plans for new Holyrood powers fall short of recommendations made by the cross-party backed Smith Commission, a report by MSPs has said.
text_ai: The Devolution (Further Powers) Committee said the UK government's draft legislation did not meet the "spirit or substance" of Smith. The Smith Commission itself was established in the wake of the 2014 Scottish independence referendum, with a clear mandate to forge a cross-party consensus on further devolution of powers to the Scottish Parliament. In response to the committee's report, a Scotland Office spokesman reiterated the UK government's "unwavering commitment" to delivering the Smith Agreement in full. title: One of the world's largest pulp and paper producers announced on Wednesday that it had stopped clearing forests as part of its operations - but the battle to stop deforestation is still far from won, as Alice Budisatrijo reports from Jakarta.

text_ai: Three of the cars went up in flames after the smash on the southbound junction of the motorway last night. One woman was pulled from a flaming car by an off-duty paramedic who ran to her aid. A 52-year-old man from Exmouth, Devon, has been arrested on suspicion of death by dangerous driving, police say. The West Midlands Ambulance Service confirmed one person was pronounced dead at the scene despite paramedic efforts. The identity of the deceased has not yet been formally released, but police are working to inform next of kin. A further five people were injured. Two patients were taken to Worcestershire Royal Hospital, while three others, including the woman rescued from the burning car, were transported to the Queen Elizabeth Hospital Birmingham. Her condition is described as serious but stable. Multiple ambulance crews, including a MERIT trauma doctor and the Hazardous Area Response Team (HART), were dispatched. West Mercia Police immediately closed the M42 southbound between Junctions 2 (Alvechurch) and 3 (Portway), with diversions via the A441 and A435. The northbound carriageway, temporarily closed for emergency access, has since reopened. The southbound section is expected to remain closed for several hours into this morning's rush hour, as collision investigators examine the scene and recovery work is completed. Hereford & Worcester Fire and Rescue Service confirmed three crews from Redditch and Bromsgrove attended, tackling "well-developed fires" involving three cars. They used specialist cutting equipment to free trapped casualties and worked to make the scene safe, describing it as "extremely challenging." West Mercia Police have launched a "thorough and extensive" investigation. Officers are appealing for anyone who witnessed the incident, or has dashcam footage, to come forward. The 52-year-old man arrested remains in police custody.

title: Saturn's ice-crusted moon Enceladus may now be the single best place to go to look for life beyond Earth.
text_ai: The assessment comes on the heels of new observations at the 500km-wide world made by the Cassini probe. The assessment comes on the heels of new observations at the 500km-wide world made by the Cassini probe. It has flown through and sampled the waters from a subsurface ocean that is being jetted into space. Cassini’s chemistry analysis strongly suggests the Enceladean seafloor has hot fluid vents - places that on Earth are known to teem with life. Cassini, a joint mission between NASA, ESA, and the Italian Space Agency, spent 13 years orbiting Saturn, making numerous passes through the plumes erupting from Enceladus’s south polar region. These plumes are essentially sprays of ice grains and water vapour originating from a global ocean hidden beneath a thick ice shell, estimated to be 20-25km deep. During its closest encounters, some just 50km above the surface, Cassini directly "tasted" these plumes, using its onboard mass spectrometers to analyse their composition. The key findings included the detection of molecular hydrogen (H2), along with significant amounts of methane (CH4) and carbon dioxide (CO2). Crucially, earlier observations by Cassini had also revealed microscopic particles of silica, which scientists interpreted as evidence of hot water reacting with rock on the seafloor. On Earth, these silica particles are a tell-tale sign of hydrothermal vents, where superheated water percolates through cracks in the crust, dissolving minerals and carrying them upwards. Dr J. Hunter Waite, a lead author on one of the seminal Cassini studies from the Southwest Research Institute, explained the significance of the gas detections: "Molecular hydrogen is like food for microbes. The amount of hydrogen we detected suggests there's a chemical disequilibrium that could provide energy for life." On our own planet, deep-sea hydrothermal vents, often called "black smokers," support thriving ecosystems entirely independent of sunlight. Here, chemosynthetic microbes form the base of the food chain, utilising chemical energy from the vents to produce organic matter. The discovery of similar conditions on Enceladus, specifically the presence of hydrogen alongside CO2 and methane, strongly implies a potential energy source for chemosynthetic life. The energy driving this geological activity is believed to be tidal heating. Enceladus orbits Saturn in an eccentric path, meaning its distance from the gas giant varies. This gravitational tugging causes the moon to flex and stretch, generating internal friction and heat. This heat melts subsurface ice, creating the ocean, and also warms the rocky core, leading to the hydrothermal reactions. "It's a perfect storm of conditions," says Professor Alice Smith, a planetary scientist at the University of Cambridge. "You have liquid water, a rocky core, and a clear energy source. That's a very compelling trifecta for habitability." For decades, Jupiter's moon Europa was considered the prime candidate for extraterrestrial life within our solar system, also believed to harbour a subsurface ocean. While Europa remains a tantalising prospect, Enceladus now presents a unique advantage: its ocean is directly accessible. "With Europa, we suspect similar processes are at play, but we haven't been able to directly sample its ocean," Professor Smith elaborates. "Enceladus is literally spraying its secrets into space, making it much easier to investigate." Titan, another Saturnian moon, boasts vast lakes and seas, but these are composed of liquid methane and ethane, not water, making it a different kind of astrobiological target focused on exotic chemistry. The direct evidence of water, energy, and organic chemistry, all readily available for sampling, positions Enceladus at the forefront of the search. The findings challenge the traditional "Goldilocks zone" concept, which primarily focuses on planets orbiting stars at a distance where liquid water can exist on the surface. Enceladus demonstrates that internal heat sources can create habitable environments far from the Sun, expanding the potential locations for life dramatically. "This isn't about finding little green men," clarifies Dr Emma Davies, an astrobiologist at the Open University. "This is about understanding the fundamental requirements for life to emerge. If life can start in these deep, dark, chemically rich environments on Enceladus, it significantly increases the probability of life existing elsewhere in the universe." The discovery shifts the focus from merely finding water to finding environments where water, energy, and the necessary chemical building blocks coexist in a dynamic way. While Cassini's mission concluded in 2017 with a dramatic plunge into Saturn's atmosphere, its legacy has spurred intense interest in follow-up missions. Scientists are now actively developing concepts for probes specifically designed to return to Enceladus, not just to sample the plumes again, but to look for definitive signs of life. One proposed mission, tentatively named the Enceladus Orbilander, would orbit the moon, analyse the plumes with even more sensitive instruments, and then potentially land on the surface to collect samples for return to Earth, or conduct in-situ analysis. Such missions would carry highly sophisticated mass spectrometers capable of detecting complex organic molecules – biomarkers – that could indicate the presence of microbial life. The challenges are immense. Any future spacecraft would need to be meticulously sterilised to prevent terrestrial contamination, and its instruments would need to be robust enough to operate in the harsh radiation environment near Saturn. Furthermore, identifying what constitutes an unequivocal "biosignature" in an extraterrestrial sample is a complex scientific and philosophical debate. Scientists would be looking for patterns of molecules, isotopic ratios, or cellular structures that are highly unlikely to arise from non-biological processes. "It's not enough to find organic molecules; we know those can form abiotically," explains Dr Davies. "We need to find evidence of biological processing, like specific chiral preferences in amino acids or complex polymeric structures. It would be the discovery of the century." The revelations from Enceladus mark a pivotal moment in humanity's quest to answer one of its oldest questions: are we alone? By pinpointing a location with such strong indicators of habitability and direct accessibility, Cassini has not only reshaped our understanding of the solar system but has also provided a clear target for the next generation of astrobiological exploration. The icy moon, once an obscure speck in Saturn's retinue, has transformed into a beacon, beckoning us to delve deeper into its hidden ocean and potentially uncover the universe's most profound secret.

title: Britain's farmers have said Tesco's fresh produce labelled with "fictional farm" brands may be misleading.
text_ai: Despite the British sounding names, the "farms" do not exist and the produce is often sourced from abroad. The National Farmers' Union (NFU) says the labels may give customers a false idea of where the produce is sourced. The National Farmers' Union (NFU) says the labels may give customers a false idea of where the produce is sourced. The NFU's president, Minette Batters, articulated concerns that the branding strategy undermined consumer confidence in the origin of food, especially at a time when shoppers are increasingly keen to support British agriculture. She highlighted that names like 'Woodside Farms' or 'Rosedene Farms' evoke images of traditional British farms, leading customers to assume the produce is domestically grown, even when it might have travelled from thousands of miles away. In response, Tesco stated that the 'farm brands' were developed to offer 'great quality, affordable produce' and to provide customers with 'simple, clear and consistent branding across categories'. A spokesperson for the supermarket giant insisted that the country of origin is always clearly displayed on the packaging, in line with legal requirements. They added that the intention was never to mislead but to create a 'strong identity' for products that are often sourced from multiple countries throughout the year to ensure availability. The brands in question, which include 'Woodside Farms' for fresh meat, 'Boswell Farms' for beef, 'Rosedene Farms' for fresh produce, and 'Nightingale Farms' for poultry, were introduced in 2016. At the time, they replaced Tesco's 'Value' range and were positioned as a value-tier offering. Consumer watchdog Which? has previously called for greater transparency in food labelling, echoing the NFU's sentiment that such branding could cause confusion. While acknowledging that the country of origin is technically present, Which? noted that prominent 'farm' names could overshadow this information, particularly for hurried shoppers. The debate highlights a broader tension within the food industry between marketing strategies and the demand for clear, unambiguous information about food sourcing. Farmers argue that ambiguity harms their ability to differentiate their domestically grown produce and secure fair prices, especially when faced with cheaper imports marketed under seemingly local guises. The NFU has urged all retailers to review their labelling practices to ensure absolute clarity for consumers, advocating for a system where origin is paramount. The Food Standards Agency (FSA) monitors food labelling for accuracy and compliance with regulations, though it has not yet issued a specific ruling on these particular brands. However, the ongoing discussion underscores the importance of transparent food supply chains and the potential for marketing to inadvertently blur the lines of provenance.

title: Bottom side Dundee won only their second Scottish Premiership game of the season and moved to within two points of opponents Hamilton Academical.
text_ai: Neither side made a breakthrough in the first half, Greg Docherty and Alexandre D'Acol firing wide for Accies. The visitors' Craig Wighton should have scored after going clean through but was also off target. However, Paul McGowan ended the impasse when his low shot evaded a clutch of players in the Hamilton box. McGowan’s strike, unleashed from just inside the area after a clever flick-on from Kenny Miller, threaded its way through a maze of legs, leaving Hamilton goalkeeper Gary Woods unsighted and unable to react in time. The ball nestled into the bottom corner, sparking jubilant scenes among the travelling support and a palpable sense of relief in the Dundee dugout. The goal, arriving just five minutes before the interval, provided a vital psychological lift for the visitors, who had endured a challenging opening period. Hamilton, stunned by the sudden setback, attempted an immediate response. Greg Docherty, a livewire throughout the first half, saw a speculative effort from 25 yards sail harmlessly over the bar, while Alexandre D'Acol, frustrated by Dundee's compact defence, found himself increasingly isolated upfront. The home side’s creative spark seemed to dim after conceding, their earlier fluidity replaced by a more frantic, less incisive approach. Dundee, meanwhile, saw out the remaining minutes of the half with composure, McGowan’s goal transforming their demeanour from tentative to determined. The second half began with Hamilton pressing for an equaliser, their manager Martin Canning clearly having demanded a sharper attacking edge during the break. Dougie Imrie, normally a reliable source of energy and crosses from the wing, was particularly active, attempting to drive his team forward. A succession of corners and free-kicks were won in dangerous areas, but Dundee's newly bolstered defence, marshalled expertly by the experienced Darren O'Dea, stood firm. Jack Hamilton, in the Dundee goal, commanded his area with authority, confidently plucking crosses out of the air and punching away others under pressure. Despite Accies’ increased urgency, their final ball often lacked the precision required to unlock Dundee. David Templeton, introduced early in the second half for the less effective D'Acol, injected some much-needed pace and trickery into Hamilton’s attack. His mazy run through the heart of the Dundee midfield in the 58th minute created space for Ali Crawford, whose powerful shot from the edge of the box was well-blocked by the lunging Cammy Kerr. The rebound fell kindly for Docherty, but his follow-up effort skewed wide, much to the frustration of the home fans. As Hamilton pushed higher up the pitch, they inevitably left gaps at the back, a risk Dundee were keen to exploit. The visitors, now playing with a newfound confidence, began to launch sharp counter-attacks, often spearheaded by the tireless Craig Wighton and the veteran Miller. In the 67th minute, Dundee doubled their lead with a goal that encapsulated their renewed vigour and Hamilton’s growing desperation. Jesse Curran, latching onto a loose ball in midfield, drove forward purposefully before unleashing a fierce, swerving shot from 20 yards. The ball dipped late, catching Gary Woods off guard and flying into the top corner, leaving the Hamilton keeper with no chance. It was a moment of individual brilliance that sent the away fans into raptures and dealt a crushing blow to Hamilton's hopes. The second goal visibly deflated Accies. Their heads seemed to drop, and the earlier intensity of their play waned. Manager Martin Canning made his final change, bringing on Rakish Bingham for the visibly tiring Imrie, but the substitutions failed to stem the tide of Dundee's momentum. The visitors, now two goals to the good, played with a freedom and swagger that belied their bottom-of-the-table status. They maintained possession intelligently, forcing Hamilton to chase shadows and conserve their energy for the final push. Hamilton did not surrender entirely. In the dying minutes, they threw everything forward in a desperate attempt to salvage something from the game. A goalmouth scramble in the 88th minute saw shots from Bingham and Templeton blocked by a wall of Dundee defenders, before Jack Hamilton bravely dived at the feet of Crawford to smother the ball. The final whistle, when it eventually came, was met with a cacophony of relief from the Dundee faithful and a groan of frustration from the Hamilton support. For Dundee, this was more than just three points; it was a statement of intent. The victory, only their second in the Scottish Premiership this season, hauled them off the foot of the table and, crucially, moved them to within two points of their opponents, Hamilton Academical. The gap, which had seemed daunting just weeks ago, now looked surmountable, injecting fresh hope into their survival bid. Manager Jim McIntyre, appointed in October, had finally seen his side deliver a performance that combined defensive solidity with clinical finishing – a blueprint for their remaining fixtures. Paul McGowan, whose opening goal set the tone, was instrumental throughout, his experience and work rate proving invaluable. Jesse Curran’s spectacular second goal will undoubtedly live long in the memory of the travelling support. Conversely, for Hamilton, the defeat represented a significant setback. Having held a comfortable mid-table position for much of the early season, their recent form has seen them slide down the standings. This home loss to their direct relegation rivals further intensified the pressure on Martin Canning and his squad. Their inability to convert chances and a susceptibility to counter-attacks will be a major concern. With other teams around them picking up points, Accies now find themselves firmly embroiled in the relegation dogfight, a position they will be desperate to escape. The prospect of a prolonged battle at the bottom looms large, and their upcoming fixtures against similarly struggling sides will be pivotal in determining their Premiership future. The result has undoubtedly reshaped the landscape at the bottom of the Scottish Premiership, igniting a relegation battle that promises to be fiercely contested in the coming weeks. Dundee's long road to redemption has taken a significant turn, while Hamilton must quickly regroup to avoid being dragged further into the mire.

title: Bury moved six points clear of the League One drop zone after a home win over 10-man Bristol Rovers.
text_ai: Stuart Sinclair handed the hosts the initiative when the Pirates midfielder was sent off in the 39th minute after being booked twice for simulation. Bury then broke the deadlock with a 50th-minute penalty by James Vaughan before Greg Leigh and half-time substitute George Miller ensured the Shakers' ended Rovers' nine-match unbeaten run. The contest at Gigg Lane began with a tense atmosphere, reflecting the high stakes for both sides. Bury, battling to distance themselves from the League One trapdoor, showed early intent, pressing high and attempting to disrupt Rovers' rhythm. The visitors, riding a wave of confidence from their impressive unbeaten streak, looked to assert their customary passing game, with midfielder Ollie Clarke and striker Ellis Harrison probing the home defence. Chasing a loose ball into the Bury penalty area, the midfielder went to ground under minimal contact, appealing vehemently for a spot-kick. Mr Kettle, however, was in no doubt, immediately brandishing a second yellow card followed by a red, sending the Rovers man for an early shower. The decision drew an angry reaction from the Rovers bench and travelling fans, but the referee's resolve was firm. Bury manager Ryan Lowe immediately urged his players to capitalise on their numerical advantage, while Rovers boss Darrell Clarke was left to reorganise his depleted side. The Shakers wasted little time in making their extra man count after the restart. Just five minutes into the second half, a surging run from Bury winger Chris Dagnall saw him brought down inside the box by Rovers defender Tom Lockyer. The penalty decision was swift and clear. Up stepped James Vaughan, who calmly dispatched the ball past Smith, sending the goalkeeper the wrong way and igniting Gigg Lane. It was a crucial breakthrough, easing the pressure on the home side and giving them a tangible reward for their improved second-half intensity. With the lead established, Bury began to play with greater freedom. The second goal arrived in the 67th minute, a testament to their persistence. A well-worked move down the left flank saw substitute George Miller, introduced at half-time for Rohan Ince, deliver a precise low cross into the box. Greg Leigh, arriving late from left-back, met the ball with a powerful first-time finish that flew into the net, leaving Smith with no chance. The goal doubled Bury's advantage and visibly deflated the 10-man Rovers, who had struggled to contain the hosts' wider play since the red card. The victory was then sealed in the 79th minute by Miller, completing a superb individual contribution from the young striker. Picking up the ball just outside the area, Miller drove towards goal, evading a challenge before unleashing a fierce shot that nestled in the bottom corner. It was a clinical finish that underscored Bury's dominance and confirmed a comprehensive win against a side that had previously been so resilient. Darrell Clarke's side, despite the numerical disadvantage, showed glimpses of their attacking prowess, particularly in the first half. However, going down to 10 men proved an insurmountable obstacle. While they attempted to push forward after falling behind, the energy expended in covering the extra ground took its toll. Clarke later expressed his frustration with the officiating, particularly the red card incident, stating, "We felt the decision was harsh, especially for a second yellow. It completely changed the game. We're disappointed to lose the unbeaten run, but we'll learn from this." The defeat halts Rovers' impressive run and sees them slip slightly in the tightly contested mid-table, though their playoff hopes remain very much alive. For Bury, this was a vital three points in their quest for League One survival. Manager Ryan Lowe lauded his team's performance, particularly their ability to maintain focus and exploit the advantage. "We knew this was a huge game," Lowe commented. "The lads showed fantastic character after the red card to go out and take the game to them. James Vaughan's penalty was pivotal, and the way we finished our chances was excellent. George Miller made a real impact off the bench. This result gives us a massive boost and shows what we're capable of." The win moves Bury six points clear of the relegation zone, providing a much-needed cushion and a surge of confidence as they enter the crucial final weeks of the season. The result marked Bury's first home win in five matches, a statistic that underlines the importance of this victory. The Shakers demonstrated a clinical edge in front of goal that had sometimes been lacking, converting key opportunities. Bristol Rovers, for their part, will rue the early dismissal that ultimately undermined their efforts to extend their impressive unbeaten streak. title: As the first month of the year draws to a close, the FA Cup reaches round four and the last 32 teams in the hat.
text_ai: Last season's fourth round produced two seismic football shocks. Premier League Chelsea were knocked out by League One Bradford at Stamford Bridge and Manchester City were dumped out by Championship Middlesbrough. BBC Sport takes a look at four ties where Premier League sides will hope to avoid away-day embarrassment this time around. ### Brighton & Hove Albion v Arsenal Arguably the most intriguing all-south-coast encounter sees Premier League giants Arsenal travel to the Amex Stadium to face Championship high-flyers Brighton & Hove Albion. While the Seagulls may not be a non-league outfit, their impressive form in the second tier, coupled with Arsenal's often-documented vulnerabilities on the road, makes this tie a genuine banana skin for Arsène Wenger's men. Brighton, under the astute guidance of manager Chris Hughton, sit comfortably in the Championship play-off places and boast one of the division's meanest defences. Their home record this season has been formidable, turning the Amex into a fortress where few visiting teams leave with maximum points. Key to their success has been the organised midfield pairing and the clinical finishing of their attackers, who will undoubtedly be relishing the opportunity to test themselves against top-flight opposition. For Arsenal, the FA Cup holds a special significance, having lifted the trophy numerous times in recent memory. However, their away form in domestic cup competitions can be a cause for concern for their faithful. Wenger will be acutely aware of the need to field a strong side, balancing the demands of the Premier League and Champions League with the potential for an embarrassing exit. The prospect of an early goal for the hosts, fueled by a raucous home crowd, could quickly turn this into a very uncomfortable afternoon for the Gunners. History shows that Arsenal have fallen victim to lower-league opposition in the past, and Brighton will be hoping to write their own chapter in the competition's rich folklore. ### Sheffield Wednesday v Tottenham Hotspur Another Premier League side facing a stern test away from home is Tottenham Hotspur, who journey north to take on Championship side Sheffield Wednesday at Hillsborough. This fixture pits two clubs with considerable FA Cup pedigree against each other, though it is Spurs who arrive as the overwhelming favourites on paper. Mauricio Pochettino's Tottenham have enjoyed a largely successful season, establishing themselves as contenders for European qualification in the Premier League. Their dynamic, high-pressing style of play has won many admirers, and with attacking talents, they possess the firepower to trouble any defence. However, the FA Cup often throws up unique challenges, and a trip to Hillsborough is precisely one of them. Sheffield Wednesday, under their new managerial regime, have shown flashes of brilliance in the Championship. While their league position may not be as lofty as Brighton's, their passionate fanbase and the intimidating atmosphere they can generate at home make them a formidable opponent on their day. The Owls will see this as a perfect opportunity to reignite their season and provide their supporters with a memorable cup run. Their physical approach and direct play could pose problems for a Spurs side that sometimes struggles against teams that deny them space and time on the ball. The pressure on Tottenham to deliver silverware remains a constant narrative, and a slip-up here would undoubtedly intensify that scrutiny. ### Preston North End v Everton The FA Cup fourth round also takes us to Deepdale, where League One promotion hopefuls Preston North End host Premier League outfit Everton. This tie offers a classic 'David and Goliath' narrative, with Preston, a club steeped in football history as the original 'Invincibles', looking to upset a top-flight side desperate for a good cup run. Everton's season has been a mixed bag, with periods of impressive form interspersed with frustrating inconsistencies. Manager Roberto Martinez will view the FA Cup as a genuine chance for his side to lift some silverware and provide a much-needed boost to their campaign. They possess a squad brimming with international talent, capable of dominating matches against lower-league opposition. However, their away performances have sometimes lacked the necessary conviction, and they've been known to struggle against well-organised, resilient teams. Preston North End, meanwhile, are enjoying a strong season in League One and are firmly in contention for promotion. Managed by a pragmatic coach, they are known for their disciplined defence and ability to hit teams on the counter-attack. Deepdale can be a tricky venue for visiting teams, especially when packed with an expectant crowd buzzing for a cup upset. For the Lilywhites, this is a chance to test themselves against Premier League quality, earn vital revenue, and potentially create a moment that will be talked about for years to come. The romance of the FA Cup is often found in such encounters, where the passion and belief of the underdog can sometimes overcome the perceived superiority of the favourite. ### Burton Albion v West Ham United Perhaps the biggest potential gulf between the two sides comes in the form of West Ham United's trip to League Two side Burton Albion. The Brewers, a club that has enjoyed a meteoric rise through the football pyramid in recent years, will be hoping to pull off the shock of the round against a West Ham side that has ambitions of its own in the Premier League. Slaven Bilić's West Ham have been one of the surprises of the Premier League season, playing an exciting brand of football that has seen them pick up notable victories against established top-flight teams. Their squad depth and quality should, on paper, be more than enough to navigate a tricky away tie against a League Two opponent. However, the FA Cup has a habit of humbling even the most confident of teams, especially when faced with the unique challenges of a compact, lower-league stadium and a highly motivated opposition. Burton Albion, under the shrewd management of a former Premier League player, have continued their impressive trajectory. They are well-drilled, resilient, and will treat this fixture as their cup final. The Pirelli Stadium, with its relatively small capacity, will be bouncing, creating an intense atmosphere that can sometimes unnerve visiting Premier League players. For the Brewers, this is an opportunity to put their club firmly on the national stage, and the financial rewards of a deep cup run would be transformative for a club of their stature. West Ham will need to be fully focused from the first whistle, avoid any complacency, and match Burton's intensity if they are to prevent a genuine giant-killing from unfolding. ### The Enduring Allure of the Cup These four ties merely scratch the surface of a fourth round packed with potential drama. Beyond the specific match-ups, the enduring allure of the FA Cup lies in its unpredictability and its capacity to deliver moments of pure footballing magic. For the smaller clubs, these fixtures represent not just a chance for glory, but a vital financial injection that can sustain them for seasons to come. The television revenue, gate receipts, and potential for a money-spinning replay against a big club can be transformative, allowing them to invest in facilities, youth development, or strengthen their playing squad. For the Premier League managers, the competition presents a different kind of pressure. While some may view it as a distraction from league priorities, an FA Cup run can galvanise a squad, build momentum, and offer the tangible reward of silverware. Conversely, an early exit, particularly at the hands of lower-league opposition, can be a significant blow to morale, invite criticism, and add unwelcome pressure to an already demanding season. The memory of Bradford City's stunning victory over Chelsea last year, or Middlesbrough's dominant display against Manchester City, serves as a potent reminder that reputations count for little once the whistle blows. It underscores the belief that on any given day, under the right circumstances, the underdog can triumph. As the fourth round approaches, fans across the country will be hoping for more of those seismic shocks, those moments that define the FA Cup and cement its place as the world's most cherished domestic cup competition. The stage is set for another weekend of upsets, drama, and the beautiful unpredictability of football.

text_ai: Supporters held a minute's applause 10 minutes into the club's Championship game against Huddersfield Town.
